title: Hospitality Across Asymmetric Means
paragraphs: Traditional hospitality etiquette, emphasizing generous provision for guests regardless of host's means, faces genuine complication within contemporary contexts of substantial economic disparity, where reciprocal hospitality expectations may impose disproportionate burden on hosts with considerably fewer resources than their guests.

This complication becomes particularly acute within cross-class friendships and family relationships, where wealthier participants may remain genuinely unaware of the proportional sacrifice traditional hospitality expectations impose on less wealthy relatives or friends.

Some argue that genuine etiquette requires wealthier participants actively acknowledging and adjusting for this asymmetry, perhaps by declining excessive hospitality or reciprocating in ways that do not require comparable financial outlay from less wealthy hosts.

Others counter that this well-intentioned adjustment risks its own form of condescension, potentially denying less wealthy hosts the dignity and agency of extending generous hospitality according to their own genuine preference and cultural values.

Navigating this tension likely requires attentive, relationship-specific judgment rather than universal rule, since appropriate response depends considerably on whether hospitality reflects genuine host preference or unspoken social pressure the host may feel unable to comfortably decline.

This attentiveness, while requiring more effort than either extreme of unreflective traditional expectation or presumptuous adjustment, likely serves genuine relational respect better than either alternative applied uniformly regardless of specific relational context and individual preference.
